In screw theory, a screw (FR: torseur) is a pair of related three dimensional vectors. It is used as an analytic tool in rigid body motions.<ref>{{#cite:Q1848}}</ref>

== History ==

In the 1830s, French mathematician [[Person:Michel Chasles|Michel Chasles]] demonstrated that any rigid body displacement can be decomposed into a rotation about a unique axis combined with a translation. This idea laid the foundation for Irish astronomer [[Person:Robert Ball|Robert Ball]] to systematise the idea into structured algebra in his 1900 treatise ''A Treatise on the Theory of Screws''. His work has since be modernised to form the modern screw theory based on dual-vectors.<ref>{{#cite:Q1860}}</ref>

== Mathematical definition ==

Let $\vec{R}$, $\vec M$ be vectors of $\mathbb R^3$

=== Classic screw ===

If for arbitrary points in space $A,B$:

$$
\vec R_B=\vec R_A \\
\vec{M_B}=\vec M_A+ \overrightarrow{BA}\times \vec{R}
$$

Then $\mathcal{\{T\}}=\left\{\begin{matrix}\vec R \\ \vec M\end{matrix}\right\}$ is a '''screw''' in this space. $\vec{R}$ is called the '''resultant''', and $\vec M_A$ the '''moment''' at $A$.<ref>{{#cite:Q1851}}</ref>

<blockquote>
Notice:

* The resultant is spatially-independent,
** i.e., it is the same at every point in space;
* The moment is spatially-dependent,
** i.e., a change in reference point results in a change in moment.
</blockquote>

=== Integrated screw ===

Let $dP$ be the measure element of system $K$ at $P$, then for an arbitrary point in space $A$

$$
\{\mathcal{U}\}_A=
\begin{Bmatrix}
\displaystyle \int_K \vec{R}(P)\,dP \\[6pt]
\displaystyle \int_K \overrightarrow{AP}\times \vec{R}(P)\,dP
\end{Bmatrix}_A .
$$

is an '''integrated screw'''.

It satisfies the property:

$$
\displaystyle \int_K \overrightarrow{BP}\times \vec{R}(P)\,dP= \displaystyle \int_K \overrightarrow{AP}\times \vec{R}(P)\,dP + \overrightarrow{BA}\times \displaystyle \int_K \vec{R}(P)\,dP
$$

analogous to classic screws.

== Forces and torques ==

A '''wrench''' describes external forces on a solid or a system and their associated moments, also known as '''torques''', according to a reference point.

=== Wrench (discrete forces) ===

If a solid or system experiences $n$ external forces $\vec F_i$ each exerted on point $M_i$, its wrench '''according to reference point $A$''' is:

$$
\{\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{n}}\}_A=
\begin{Bmatrix}
\sum_{i=1}^n \vec{F}_{i} \\
\sum_{i=1}^n \overrightarrow{AM_i}\times \vec{F}_{i}
\end{Bmatrix}_A
$$

== Screw describing the motion of solid $S$ ==

=== Twist ===

'''Twist''' is the screw of the rotational velocity vector of solid $S$ according to a given reference and its associated moment vector, the linear velocity vector at a given point.

$$
\mathcal{\{V}(S/R)\}_A=\left\{\begin{matrix}\vec \omega_{S/R} \\ \vec v_{A,S/R}\end{matrix}\right\}
$$

==== Composition for complex movements ====

As motion is relative, according to a different reference system, the velocity of the solid will be different.

In general, for a point $A$ on solid $(S)$ in motion according to reference system $R_1$, its motion according to another reference system $R_0$ is:

$$
\begin{cases}
\vec \omega_{S/R_0}=\vec \omega_{S/R_1}+\vec \omega_{R_1/R_0} \\
\vec v_{A,S/R_0}=\vec v_{A,S/R_1}+\vec v_{A \in R_1/R_0}
\end{cases}
$$

where

$$
\vec v_{A \in R_1/R_0}=\vec v_{O_1,R_1/R_0}+\overrightarrow{AO_1}\times \vec \omega_{R_1/R_0}
$$

is the velocity in $R_0$ of the point of $R_1$ that coincides with $A$ at the instant considered.

Furthermore, the acceleration vector can be derived by differentiation:

$$
\vec a_{A,S/R_0}=(\frac{d\vec v_{A,S/R_0}}{dt})_{R_0}
$$

Which gives

$$
\vec a_{A,S/R_0}=\vec a_{A,S/R_1}+\vec a_{A \in R_1/R_0}+2\vec \omega_{R_1/R_0} \times \vec v_{A,S/R_1}
$$

<blockquote>
Notice that the acceleration of point $A$ according to $R_0$ is more than the sum of its acceleration according to $R_1$ and the acceleration of $R_1$ according to $R_0$ at point $A$. The additional term, $2\vec \omega_{R_1/R_0} \times \vec v_{A,S/R_1}$, is known as '''Coriolis complementary acceleration'''.
</blockquote>

where

$$
\vec a_{A \in R_1/R_0}=\vec a_{O_1,R_1/R_0}+(x_{A/R_1}\frac{d^2\vec i_1}{dt^2})_{R_0}+(y_{A/R_1}\frac{d^2\vec j_1}{dt^2})_{R_0}+(z_{A/R_1}\frac{d^2\vec k_1}{dt^2})_{R_0}
$$

<ref>{{#cite:Q1854}}</ref>

== Screws describing the motion of system $K$ ==

=== Kinetic screw ===

The '''kinetic screw''' represents the linear momentum of a system $K$ and its angular momentum according to a given reference point.<ref>{{#cite:Q3751}}{{#cite:Q1848}}</ref>

$$
\{\mathcal{K}\}_A=
\begin{Bmatrix}
\displaystyle \vec{p}=\int_K \vec{v}(M)\,dm=m\vec{v}(C) \\[6pt]
\displaystyle \vec{\sigma}_A=\int_K \overrightarrow{AM}\times \vec{v}(M)\,dm
\end{Bmatrix}_A .
$$

The rows are separate physical quantities:

* the resultant $\vec{p}$ is the '''linear momentum''' of $K$;
* the moment $\vec{\sigma}_A$ is the '''angular momentum''' of $K$ about $A$.

So the moment row is not "$\vec{p}$ taken at $A$": it is the angular momentum, which the resultant does not determine.

Here $\vec{v}(M)$ is the velocity of the mass element $dm$ in the chosen reference frame, $C$ is the centre of mass of $K$, and the identity $\int_K \vec{v}(M)\,dm=m\vec{v}(C)$ assumes the mass $m$ of $K$ is constant in time.

==== The pair is a screw ====

For arbitrary points $A,B$,

$$
\vec{\sigma}_B=\int_K \overrightarrow{BM}\times \vec{v}(M)\,dm
=\int_K \left(\overrightarrow{BA}+\overrightarrow{AM}\right)\times \vec{v}(M)\,dm
=\vec{\sigma}_A+\overrightarrow{BA}\times \vec{p},
$$

which is the transport law of [[#Classic screw|the classic screw]]. The pair $\{\mathcal{K}\}_A$ is therefore a screw, of resultant $\vec{p}$ and moment $\vec{\sigma}_A$.<ref>{{#cite:Q3751}}</ref>

==== Kinetic screw of a solid ====

For a solid $(S)$ of mass $m$ whose inertia matrix at its centre of mass $C$ is $\mathbf{I}_C$,

$$
\vec{\sigma}_A=\mathbf{I}_C\vec{\omega}+\overrightarrow{AC}\times \vec{p},
$$

so $\vec{p}$ together with the pure spin $\vec{\sigma}_C=\mathbf{I}_C\vec{\omega}$ determines the kinetic screw at every point.<ref>{{#cite:Q3751}}{{#cite:Q3749}}</ref>

=== Dynamic screw ===

The dynamic screw represents the acceleration of a system $K$ and its moment according to a given reference point.

$$
\{\mathcal{D}\}_A=
\begin{Bmatrix}
\displaystyle \int_K \vec{a}(M)\,dm=m\vec{a}(C) \\[6pt]
\displaystyle \vec{\delta}_A=\int_K \overrightarrow{AM}\times \vec{a}(M)\,dm
\end{Bmatrix}_A ,
$$

where $\vec{a}(M)$ is the acceleration of the mass element $dm$ in the chosen reference frame, $C$ is the centre of mass of $K$, and $\vec{\delta}_A$ is the '''dynamic moment''' about $A$. It obeys the same transport law as the kinetic screw.

==== Relation to the kinetic screw ====

At a point $A$ fixed in the reference frame, $\vec{a}(M)=\frac{d\vec{v}(M)}{dt}$ for every mass element $dm$, so

$$
\{\mathcal{D}\}_A=\frac{d}{dt}\{\mathcal{K}\}_A .
$$

At a moving point the moment row gains a term: differentiating $\vec{\sigma}_A$ with $A$ moving at $\vec{v}_A$ gives

$$
\vec{\delta}_A=\frac{d\vec{\sigma}_A}{dt}+\vec{v}_A\times \vec{p} .
$$

So $\{\mathcal{D}\}_A$ is the time derivative of $\{\mathcal{K}\}_A$ only when $\vec{v}_A\times\vec{p}=\vec{0}$, that is at a point fixed in the frame, at $A=C$, or at any point whose velocity is parallel to $\vec{p}$. At other points the shortcut misses $\vec{v}_A\times\vec{p}$, which is the term dropped when a moment equation is written about an accelerating point.<ref>{{#cite:Q3751}}</ref>

=== Use of the kinetic screw ===

# '''One transported pair, not two theorems.''' The momentum state of $K$ is the single pair $(\vec{p},\vec{\sigma}_A)$ at one point, and the transport law above carries it to any other point with one cross product, so nothing has to be re-derived at each new reference point.<ref>{{#cite:Q3750}}</ref>
# '''The fundamental principle of dynamics in one line.''' $\{\mathcal{D}\}_A=\{\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{ext}}\}_A$ has exactly two rows, the resultant theorem $\dot{\vec{p}}=\sum\vec{F}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and the moment theorem $\vec{\delta}_A=\sum\vec{M}_{A,\mathrm{ext}}$. The reference point is then a free parameter that deletes terms: $A=C$ deletes the transport term $\overrightarrow{AC}\times\vec{p}$, and a point on the line of action of an unknown reaction deletes that reaction from the moment row.<ref>{{#cite:Q3751}}{{#cite:Q1848}}</ref>
# '''Additivity, so internal actions cancel.''' Screws of the same kind add, so for a system $K$ made of solids $S_i$, $\{\mathcal{K}(K)\}_A=\sum_i\{\mathcal{K}(S_i)\}_A$, and likewise for $\{\mathcal{D}\}$ and $\{\mathcal{F}\}$. Summing the fundamental principle over a mechanism cancels every joint reaction pairwise by the 3rd law, which yields its equations of motion without solving for the constraint forces.<ref>{{#cite:Q3751}}{{#cite:Q3749}}</ref>
# '''Conservation as one statement.''' If the external wrench vanishes, $\dot{\vec{p}}=\vec{0}$ and $\dot{\vec{\sigma}}_A=\vec{v}_A\times\vec{p}$, so for $A$ fixed in the frame, or for $A=C$, the kinetic screw itself is constant. Conservation of linear momentum and of angular momentum then form one conservation law about one object.<ref>{{#cite:Q3750}}</ref>
# '''Dynamics as a derivative, with a moving-point caveat.''' As shown [[#Relation to the kinetic screw|above]], $\{\mathcal{D}\}_A=\frac{d}{dt}\{\mathcal{K}\}_A$ holds at a point fixed in the frame and at the centre of mass, and is otherwise off by $\vec{v}_A\times\vec{p}$.
# '''Energy and virtual power are pairings of screws.''' Two screws $\{\mathcal{A}\}_A$, $\{\mathcal{B}\}_A$ have the '''comoment''' $\{\mathcal{A}\}_A\otimes\{\mathcal{B}\}_A=\vec{R}_{\mathcal{A}}\cdot\vec{M}_{\mathcal{B},A}+\vec{M}_{\mathcal{A},A}\cdot\vec{R}_{\mathcal{B}}$, independent of the reference point, so pairing the twist of a solid with its kinetic screw gives twice its kinetic energy, $2T=\vec{v}_A\cdot\vec{p}+\vec{\omega}\cdot\vec{\sigma}_A$, whose independence from $A$ is König's decomposition at $A=C$ and the parallel-axis transport of the inertia matrix at $A\neq C$. Pairing a wrench with a twist gives the virtual power, and a pair of screws whose comoment vanishes is '''reciprocal''', i.e. that wrench does no work on that motion.<ref>{{#cite:Q3750}}{{#cite:Q3751}}</ref>
# '''An invariant and a central axis.''' $\vec{p}\cdot\vec{\sigma}_A$ does not depend on $A$, so the kinetic screw has a pitch $h=\vec{p}\cdot\vec{\sigma}_A/\|\vec{p}\|^2$, the momentum analogue of the pitch of a motion screw, and the points where $\vec{\sigma}_A\parallel\vec{p}$ form its '''central axis''', on which $\|\vec{\sigma}_A\|$ is minimal. The central axis plays the role for momentum that the instantaneous screw axis plays for motion.<ref>{{#cite:Q3750}}{{#cite:Q1848}}</ref>
# '''The 6-D form used in computation.''' In a common frame the kinetic screw is the 6-component '''spatial momentum''' and its relation to the twist is the $6\times 6$ spatial inertia, $\{\mathcal{K}\}_A=\mathcal{I}_A\{\mathcal{V}\}_A$, which is the quantity that recursive Newton-Euler, articulated-body, and composite-rigid-body algorithms operate on. Taken about the centre of mass it is the '''centroidal momentum matrix''' of momentum-based control for legged, humanoid, and free-flying robots.<ref>{{#cite:Q3749}}{{#cite:Q3754}}</ref>

== Fundamental principle of dynamics ==

The '''fundamental principle of dynamics''' states

$$
\{\mathcal{D}\}_A=\{\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{ext}}\}_A
$$

where $\{\mathcal{D}\}$ is [[#Dynamic_screw|the dynamic screw]] and $\{\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{ext}}\}_A$ is [[#Wrench_(discrete_forces)|the wrench]].
